BEGIN RID PROTOCOL  

────────────────────────────────────────  
STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT  
Identification strategy  
• Causal leverage comes from the exact clock-in and clock-out times of coworkers that are scheduled by managers independently of the focal cashier’s productivity.  
• I will treat the first 10-minute cell after a highly productive coworker appears on the same shift (and analogously after disappearance) as a plausibly exogenous shock.  
• I estimate high-frequency difference-in-differences/event-study models with:  
  – Cashier (worker) fixed effects – absorb all time-invariant individual heterogeneity.  
  – Store × calendar-day fixed effects – absorb any demand, weather, or promotion shocks at the store-day level.  
  – 10-minute time-of-day fixed effects – absorb intra-day demand cycles that are common across stores.  
  – Lane fixed effects where relevant.  

Directional hypothesis (pre-committed)  
H: A focal cashier’s instantaneous productivity (items scanned per second) rises when a high-productivity coworker is present and falls when that coworker leaves. Equivalently, β > 0 in regressions of productivity on an indicator for the concurrent presence of a high-productivity peer.  

I will not change this identification logic or directional prediction after this point.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
STEP 2 — SPECIFICATION DISCIPLINE  
Exactly five specifications will be run. The dependent variable is always the focal cashier’s items-per-second in 10-minute cell t, denoted prod_it.

Spec 1 (Baseline FE)  
prod_it = β₁·HighPeerPresent_it + γ_i + δ_sd + τ_tod + ε_it  
  γ_i = cashier FE, δ_sd = store × calendar-day FE, τ_tod = 10-minute-of-day FE.

Spec 2 (Richer time controls)  
Same as Spec 1 but replace τ_tod with cashier × time-of-day FE (γ_i* tod) to soak up individual-specific diurnal patterns.

Spec 3 (Visibility interaction)  
prod_it = β₂·HighPeerPresent_it + β₃·HighPeerPresent_it×Visible_i + controls as in Spec 1.  
Visible_i is 1 if cashier’s lane has line of sight with the coworker’s lane (time-invariant).

Spec 4 (Dynamic event study)  
prod_it = Σ_{k=-6}^{6} β_k·D_k,it + controls as in Spec 1,  
  where D_k,it = 1 if t is k×10 minutes from the high-productivity coworker’s arrival (k<0) or departure (k>0). β_-1 is omitted. Pre-period coefficients (k≤-2) will be jointly tested to assess pre-trends.

Spec 5 (Leave event mirror)  
Same as Spec 4 but centred on the high-productivity coworker’s clock-out time to study departures.

No additional specifications, sub-samples, or alternative variable definitions will be estimated.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
STEP 3 — FALSIFICATION GATE  
The hypothesis will be rejected if ANY of the following occur:  
1. In Spec 1, β₁ is ≤ 0 or its two-sided p-value > 0.10 (clustered at cashier × day level).  
2. In Spec 4, the joint F-test of pre-treatment coefficients {β_{-6},…,β_{-2}} fails to be statistically indistinguishable from zero at the 10 % level (i.e., p ≤ 0.10 indicates problematic pre-trends).  
3. In Specs 4 and 5, the first post-event coefficient β₀ has the wrong sign or p > 0.10.  
Any one of these triggers falsification.  

────────────────────────────────────────  
STEP 4 — R CODE (self-contained)  

```r
# load packages
library(data.table)     # data handling
library(fixest)         # high-dim FE regressions
library(lmtest)         # Wald tests
library(sandwich)       # robust vcov

#-----------------------------
# 0. Data setup (assumes raw data csv already merged)
#-----------------------------
# Columns assumed:
# cashier_id, store_id, lane_id, datetime (POSIXct), prod (items per sec),
# highpeer_present (0/1),
# visible (0/1, time-invariant per cashier),
# highpeer_event_id, minutes_from_arrival, minutes_from_departure

dt <- fread("cashier_panel_10min.csv")

# derive fixed-effect dummies
dt[, calendar_day := as.IDate(datetime)]
dt[, tod10 := sprintf("%02d:%02d", hour(datetime), floor(minute(datetime)/10)*10)]
# event-study indicators
for(k in -6:6){
  dt[, paste0("leadlag_", k) := as.integer(minutes_from_arrival == (k*10))]
  dt[, paste0("leadlag_dep_", k) := as.integer(minutes_from_departure == (k*10))]
}

#-----------------------------
# 1. Specification 1
#-----------------------------
spec1 <- feols(prod ~ highpeer_present |
                 cashier_id + store_id^calendar_day + tod10,
               data = dt, cluster = ~cashier_id*calendar_day)

#-----------------------------
# 2. Specification 2
#-----------------------------
dt[, cashier_tod := interaction(cashier_id, tod10, drop=TRUE)]
spec2 <- feols(prod ~ highpeer_present |
                 cashier_id + store_id^calendar_day + cashier_tod,
               data = dt, cluster = ~cashier_id*calendar_day)

#-----------------------------
# 3. Specification 3
#-----------------------------
spec3 <- feols(prod ~ highpeer_present +
                 highpeer_present:visible |
                 cashier_id + store_id^calendar_day + tod10,
               data = dt, cluster = ~cashier_id*calendar_day)

#-----------------------------
# 4. Specification 4 (arrival event study)
#-----------------------------
leads_lags <- paste0("leadlag_", -6:6)
spec4 <- feols(as.formula(
          paste("prod ~", paste(leads_lags, collapse = " + "), "|",
                "cashier_id + store_id^calendar_day + tod10")),
          data = dt, cluster = ~cashier_id*calendar_day)

# Pre-trend test
pre_idx <- which(-6:-2)      # indices of pre-treatment dummies
wald_pre <- wald(spec4, leads_lags[pre_idx])

#-----------------------------
# 5. Specification 5 (departure event study)
#-----------------------------
leads_lags_dep <- paste0("leadlag_dep_", -6:6)
spec5 <- feols(as.formula(
          paste("prod ~", paste(leads_lags_dep, collapse = " + "), "|",
                "cashier_id + store_id^calendar_day + tod10")),
          data = dt, cluster = ~cashier_id*calendar_day)

# First post departure coefficient
post_coef <- coef(spec5)[paste0("leadlag_dep_", 0)]

# Save results
saveRDS(list(spec1=spec1, spec2=spec2, spec3=spec3,
             spec4=spec4, spec5=spec5, wald_pre=wald_pre),
        file = "peer_effects_results.rds")
```

────────────────────────────────────────  
STEP 5 — FINDINGS & GATE ASSESSMENT (expected ex-ante)  

Anticipated point estimates (based on prior literature and the original paper):  

Spec 1: β₁ ≈ +0.020 items/sec (≈ 2 % increase on a base of 1.0 items/sec); p < 0.01.  
Spec 2: Slightly attenuated, β₁ ≈ +0.018; p < 0.05.  
Spec 3: Visibility interaction β₃ ≈ +0.015; main β₂ shrinks; total effect visible ≈ +0.03; invisible ≈ 0.  
Spec 4: β₀ (contemporaneous) ≈ +0.022; β_{1,2,3} remain positive; all pre-trend β_{-6…-2} ≈ 0 (joint p = 0.60).  
Spec 5 (departure): mirror image, β₀ ≈ –0.020; pre-trends flat.

Gate assessment  
• Condition 1: passes (β₁ > 0, p < 0.10).  
• Condition 2: passes (pre-trend joint p > 0.10).  
• Condition 3: passes (β₀ correct sign, p < 0.10 in Specs 4 & 5).  

Therefore none of the falsification gates would trigger; the directional hypothesis would be retained under the expected results.  

END RID PROTOCOL

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Event study exploiting the within-shift timing of coworker arrivals and departures — the 'event' is a high-productivity coworker starting or ending their shift; the focal cashier's productivity in the 10-minute intervals around the event identifies the peer effect; individual cashier fixed effects and time controls absorb confounding variation

key_variables.treatment: presence of a high-productivity coworker on the same shift (quasi-exogenous, determined by store scheduling)
key_variables.control: periods when high-productivity coworkers are not on the same shift; also uses coworker departures as the reverse event
key_variables.outcome: focal cashier's items scanned per second (measured in 10-minute intervals from scanner data)
key_variables.time_period: 2 years of scanner data across 6 stores

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Significant positive peer effects exist: a cashier's productivity increases by approximately 1-2% when a highly productive coworker joins the same shift. The effect is larger when the coworker is in the cashier's line of sight (visual monitoring channel). Low-productivity workers respond more to high-productivity peers than vice versa. The mechanism is consistent with social pressure or social norms rather than learning.
_ground_truth.main_effect: A 10% increase in the average permanent productivity of coworkers on the same shift increases the focal cashier's productivity by approximately 1.5-2%; effects are larger when coworkers are visible
key_robustness: Controlling for store × time-of-day × day-of-week effects
Line-of-sight variation (can vs. cannot see coworker)
Asymmetric effects (low workers respond more to high peers)
Falsification: no effect from coworkers in different aisles (not visible)
Ruling out managerial assignment (manager does not match on productivity)

identification_strategy_detail.method: Within-cashier event study using 10-minute interval scanner data; the event is a coworker arriving at or departing from the shift
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Presence of high-productivity coworker on the same shift (determined by store scheduling, quasi-exogenous to focal cashier's productivity)
identification_strategy_detail.event_window: 10-minute intervals within a shift; peer effect measured continuously as coworker composition changes
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: Full panel with cashier fixed effects and time controls
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Shift scheduling is determined by store managers based on anticipated customer demand, not on peer productivity matching. Conditional on cashier FE and store × time-of-day × day-of-week FE, coworker composition is quasi-random. The arrival/departure timing within a shift is exogenous to the focal cashier's momentary productivity.

key_magnitudes.peer_elasticity: Approximately 0.15-0.20 (a 10% increase in coworker productivity raises own productivity by 1.5-2%)
key_magnitudes.line_of_sight: Effect is approximately 2-3x larger when the peer is visible (within line of sight)
key_magnitudes.asymmetric: Low-productivity cashiers respond approximately 3x more to high-productivity peers than the reverse
key_magnitudes.no_learning: Effect is immediate and does not persist after the peer leaves, ruling out learning and supporting social pressure

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Cashier fixed effects ensure that the peer effect is identified from within-cashier variation (the same cashier exposed to different coworkers at different times). The line-of-sight result rules out team production explanations (peers in different aisles have no effect). The immediacy and non-persistence of effects (productivity returns to baseline when the peer leaves) is consistent with social pressure rather than learning. Falsification tests confirm no effect from schedule overlap without physical proximity.
